rv.q: The party’s over, and Scott’s extravagant loneliness is unforgettable.
So – and how! – does its stratospherically gifted leading man, Andrew Scott.
There is more, though, to this triumph than great Scott.
After a lively start, things stall with the gay love scene.
His panache fills the entire theatre.
Scott locates the substance within Coward's theatrical soufflé and manages something quite astonishing: amidst the fusillade of laughs, he opens a window on to this play's fretful heart.
It lifts a deceptively light and ludicrous comedy that, 80 years on, has retained its fizz, into something delicately profound.
The director Matthew Warchus’s richly entertaining take on the play has, in the role of Garry, a singular actor in the fast-rising TV name Andrew Scott.
His attempt to turn it into a crowd-pleasing pantomime full of high farce and big laughs must be counted a success.
Aside from being touching, beautifully staged, fantastically performed and well-observed, Present Laughter is just so, so funny.

cn.t: Andrew Scott dazzles in Matthew Warchus's gleaming revival, delivering a magnetic, elastic performance that fills the theatre with laughter. Critics mostly praise the entertaining production, though some question the gender-switch update.
